candidates.rationale: 12-1 momentum: prior return from 252 to 21 days ago, skipping the last month; underreaction to slow-diffusing news drives continuation while avoiding short-term reversal contamination.
6-1 momentum: prior return from 126 to 21 days ago, skipping the last month to strip out short-term reversal while keeping the underreaction-driven trend.
Quarter-scale momentum skipping the most recent 10 days: isolates the slower information-diffusion component of the trend from near-term liquidity noise.
Skip-2-month momentum over a 9-month lookback: firms with persistent fundamental improvement keep drifting after the initial reaction fades.
Skip-week momentum over a 1-month window: captures early-stage trend continuation once the first week's liquidity noise has passed.
Skip-2-week momentum over 2 months: gradual investor underreaction to firm news sustains the trend past the initial short-term reversal window.
Skip-month momentum over a 7-month base: a mid-length underreaction window between the classic 6-1 and 12-1 formulations.
Annual momentum skipping the most recent quarter: isolates the slowest-decaying part of the trend, least contaminated by any recent reversal.
10-day return scaled by its own volatility: a trend achieved with low risk reflects steady information-driven demand rather than noisy swings, so it persists more reliably than raw return.
1-month risk-adjusted momentum: return-per-unit-of-risk over the window separates genuine steady demand from a single volatile spike, and the former continues.
2-month risk-adjusted momentum: smoother, lower-vol trends reflect gradual repricing that under-reacting investors keep extending.
Quarterly Sharpe-style momentum: risk-adjusting the cumulative return isolates the persistent-demand component of the trend from volatility-driven noise.
Semiannual risk-adjusted momentum: a calm, steady half-year climb is more likely information-driven and durable than an equally large but choppy one.
9-month risk-adjusted momentum: return-to-variability over this horizon proxies the steadiness of institutional accumulation, which continues.
Annual risk-adjusted momentum: the classic 12-month trend, normalized by its own risk so that low-volatility grinders outrank equally-performing but erratic names.
Quarterly return scaled by a fresher 1-month volatility read: judges the trend's persistence against the current, not stale, risk backdrop.
Semiannual return scaled by recent 2-month volatility: flags trends whose current risk profile has calmed, which historically persist longer.
Monthly return scaled by a very fresh 2-week volatility read: captures whether a recent trend is currently being achieved calmly or erratically.
Annual return judged against the current quarter's volatility: a stale trend now unfolding through a calm regime is more likely to keep extending.
Percentage deviation of price from its own 10-day exponential trend: a sustained gap shows slow investors still adjusting their reference price upward, extending the move.
Deviation from a 1-month exponential trend line: persistence above trend reflects underreaction that continues to close as laggards adjust.
Deviation from a 2-month EMA: captures an established medium trend that price keeps pulling away from as demand persists.
Deviation from a quarterly EMA: a stock trading well above its own slow-moving trend line signals accelerating, self-reinforcing demand.
Deviation from a half-year EMA: a durable premium to a slow reference price reflects an established uptrend that under-reacting capital keeps extending.
Deviation from a 9-month EMA: this long a persistent premium marks a structural repricing that continues as slow capital catches up.
Deviation from an annual EMA: the most persistent trend signal, reflecting a year-long reference shift that continues to attract lagging capital.
Weekly vs monthly EMA crossover: a fast trend outpacing the slower one signals accelerating demand that tends to persist over the next several days.
2-week vs 2-month EMA crossover: an early acceleration in trend often precedes continued follow-through as more participants notice the move.
Monthly vs quarterly EMA crossover: classic trend-following turning point where short-run demand is outrunning the established base trend.
2-month vs half-year EMA crossover: a medium trend pulling ahead of the long-run trend signals a durable regime shift rather than noise.
Quarterly vs 9-month EMA crossover: captures slower-forming trend acceleration that persists as institutional rebalancing catches up.
2-week vs quarterly EMA crossover: a sharp short trend breaking away from its quarterly base often marks the start of a new leg that continues.
Monthly vs half-year EMA crossover: identifies trend acceleration relative to a slower institutional-timescale reference.
2-month vs annual EMA crossover: a medium-term trend pulling away from the year-long base signals a durable regime change that continues.
Nearness to the 63-day high: investors anchor on a recent high and underreact to further good news near it, so proximity predicts continued drift.
Nearness to the 126-day high: anchoring on a half-year reference point causes continued underreaction-driven drift for names pressing against it.
Nearness to the 189-day high: a 9-month anchor is salient enough to cause persistent underreaction, sustaining continuation near the mark.
Classic 52-week-high proximity: the most salient anchor for investors, producing the George-Hwang underreaction effect that drives continuation.
Elevation above the 63-day low: distance already travelled from a salient distress point reflects confirmed improving sentiment that keeps extending by the same anchoring logic.
Elevation above the half-year low: a larger confirmed recovery from a salient trough signals durable improving sentiment that persists.
Elevation above the 9-month low: the further price has climbed from this anchor, the more the recovery has been validated over time, extending the trend.
Elevation above the 52-week low: mirrors the 52-week-high anchoring effect from the opposite pole, rewarding confirmed multi-quarter recoveries.
Recency of the 10-day high: a high set very recently signals fresh, unresolved buying pressure not yet fully priced in, predicting near-term continuation.
Recency of the monthly high: novelty of the high matters for anchoring strength, so a fresh high predicts more continuation than a stale one.
Recency of the 2-month high: fresher highs carry more unresolved information than highs that occurred weeks ago and have since been digested.
Recency of the quarterly high: a high made in the last few days signals demand that is still actively building, unlike one set early in the quarter.
Recency of the half-year high: the longer since the high was set, the more likely the trend has already stalled, so freshness predicts persistence.
Staleness of the 10-day low: the longer since price touched bottom, the more confirmed the bounce, consistent with underreaction-driven continuation.
Staleness of the monthly low: a low set weeks ago rather than yesterday indicates a more established recovery that keeps extending.
Staleness of the 2-month low: distance in time from the trough is a cleaner recovery-confirmation signal than distance in price alone.
Staleness of the quarterly low: an old trough with no retest since suggests sellers have been fully absorbed, supporting continued recovery.
Staleness of the half-year low: a durable gap in time since the last trough marks a well-established, self-reinforcing recovery.
Information discreteness over 10 days: a trend built from a steady majority of same-sign days is underreacted to and continues, while the same return via a few jumps reverses (frog-in-the-pan).
Monthly information discreteness: consistent grinding trends are priced in gradually and persist, whereas jump-driven moves of the same size are already fully reflected and stall.
2-month information discreteness: the ratio of consistent to discrete days achieving the same cumulative move predicts whether underreaction still has room to run.
Quarterly information discreteness: a smooth quarter-long climb signals gradual diffusion of good news that continues, unlike a lumpy one driven by a few prints.
Half-year information discreteness: sustained day-by-day consistency over two quarters is a stronger continuation signal than an equal return from sporadic jumps.
9-month information discreteness: the longest-window consistency measure, capturing whether a slow trend has been a steady grind that keeps underreacted-to.
2-day reversal: an ultra-short cumulative return mostly proxies transient order-flow and bid-ask bounce rather than news, so it mean-reverts almost immediately.
3-day reversal: short-horizon price pressure reflects liquidity demand that market makers get compensated for absorbing, causing a quick bounce-back.
1-week reversal: weekly cumulative moves in large caps are dominated by transient flow rather than new fundamental information, so they revert.
8-day reversal: captures the tail end of the short-term overreaction window before medium-term momentum effects begin to dominate.
3-day overreaction amplified when today's volume ranks high in its own 15-day history: moves on abnormally heavy volume are more likely forced or liquidity-driven flow and revert harder.
Weekly overreaction amplified by a high volume percentile over the past month: heavy-volume weekly moves reflect crowded, unstable positioning that mean-reverts.
3-day overreaction scaled by volume's percentile in a tight 10-day window: isolates unusually intense short-term participation as the driver of the reversal.
Weekly overreaction scaled against a longer 50-day volume history: a move that is abnormal even relative to a broad baseline is the strongest reversal candidate.

Open-price gap relative to the close 2 sessions earlier captures multi-session drift into the open; dislocations from a stale reference price tend to partially correct as the session's liquidity is supplied.
Gap versus the close 3 sessions back: a large pre-open dislocation from an aging reference price reflects order-imbalance that fades as normal trading resumes.
Gap versus the close a week back: a wide open-price dislocation from a week-old anchor is more likely a temporary imbalance than a repriced fundamental, and it corrects.
Position of the close within its 5-day range: pinned near the top reflects persistent buying pressure that continues into the next session.
Position within the 10-day range: a close near the range top signals sustained demand that tends to persist over the following days.
Monthly stochastic position: a close consistently pinned high in its range reflects persistent buying pressure that continues, low reflects persistent selling.
2-month range position: a stock grinding near the top of a 2-month range shows demand that has not yet been exhausted.
Quarterly range position: sustained proximity to the top of a 3-month range reflects durable accumulation that continues.
Percentile rank of the close within its trailing 10-day distribution: a stock grinding to new local highs shows a strength pattern that tends to continue.
Percentile rank of the close within its own trailing month: persistently high percentile ranks reflect an uptrend investors are slow to fully price.
Percentile position within a 2-month self-history: a stock spending most of its time near its own recent ceiling is displaying durable relative strength.
Percentile position within a quarterly self-history: captures medium-horizon trend strength independent of the stock's absolute volatility scale.
Percentile position within a half-year self-history: identifies stocks in a slow, durable uptrend relative to their own longer-run trading range.
10-day range position scaled by realised volatility: the same relative position in the range is a stronger, less noisy directional signal when achieved under low volatility.
Monthly range position scaled by volatility: a high percentile position reached calmly is more informative of genuine demand than one reached amid turbulence.
2-month range position scaled by volatility: filters out range-topping moves that are really just an artifact of a generally noisy trading regime.
Price z-score vs its own 2-month mean and volatility: a sustained deviation over this horizon reflects an established trend that continues as under-reacting investors adjust gradually.
Quarterly price z-score: a durable deviation from the 3-month mean signals a trend investors have not fully repriced, so it continues.
Half-year price z-score: sustained deviation from a slow reference mean reflects an established regime shift that keeps extending.
9-month price z-score: this long a persistent gap from the mean marks a structural trend that under-reacting capital keeps chasing.
Annual price z-score: the slowest-forming trend-strength measure, reflecting a year-long repricing that continues to attract lagging capital.
5-day price z-score, inverted: at this short horizon a large deviation from the mean mostly reflects a transient liquidity shock that reverts within days.
10-day price z-score, inverted: extreme short-run deviations are dominated by noise rather than repricing and bounce back toward the mean.
10-day price-participation correlation: a rising price with rising dollar volume confirms genuine demand and predicts continuation, versus a rise on fading volume.
Monthly price-volume trend correlation: healthy uptrends are accompanied by growing participation, a pattern more durable than a price rise on thinning interest.
2-month price-volume correlation: sustained co-movement of price and dollar volume over this horizon signals broad-based, not narrow, participation in the trend.
Quarterly price-volume correlation: a durable positive relationship over 3 months indicates the trend is being confirmed by real capital flow, not a handful of prints.
10-day return-volume correlation: positive co-movement indicates buying pressure driving price on real demand rather than thin, noisy trading, a pattern that persists.
Monthly return-volume correlation: gains made alongside rising volume reflect conviction buying that continues, distinct from a drift on quiet, indecisive trading.
2-month return-volume correlation: a durable positive link between daily gains and participation signals an accumulating position that keeps building.
Quarterly momentum discounted when 1-month realised volatility has been rising, a classic precursor to momentum crashes; the term stays positive only when the volatility backdrop is calming.
Half-year momentum discounted by a rising 2-month volatility trend: keeps exposure aligned with the calm-volatility regime in which trends are known to persist rather than crash.
Quarterly momentum weighted down when 2-month volatility is climbing: avoids riding trends into a deteriorating risk backdrop that historically precedes reversals.
Half-year momentum filtered by very recent (1-month) volatility acceleration: a sudden vol spike late in a long trend is the textbook setup for a momentum crash to avoid.
10-day upside vs downside volatility gap: when upside dispersion dominates, recent gains reflect broad-based buying rather than a few sharp down-spikes, a healthier pattern that persists.
Monthly volatility asymmetry: a stock whose up-days are more dispersed than its down-days is rallying on strength rather than merely failing to crash, and continues.
2-month volatility asymmetry: sustained dominance of upside dispersion signals a healthier volatility profile associated with more durable uptrends.
Quarterly volatility asymmetry: a persistent skew toward upside dispersion over 3 months reflects broad participation in gains rather than occasional panic selling.

Quarterly momentum discounted by leverage: highly levered firms face greater distress and refinancing risk that makes their trends fragile, so momentum persists more reliably among low-leverage firms.
Half-year momentum discounted by leverage: balance-sheet risk raises the odds of a sudden reversal, so the continuation signal is weaker for highly levered names.
Annual momentum discounted by leverage: a full year of gains is more trustworthy as durable when the firm is not simultaneously carrying elevated financial risk.
3-day reversal filtered by accrual quality: firms with earnings running ahead of cash flow are more prone to sentiment-driven overreaction and mean-revert more reliably than low-accrual names.
Weekly reversal filtered by accrual quality: high-accrual firms' short-term price swings better reflect sentiment than fundamentals, making the bounce-back more reliable.
8-day reversal filtered by accrual quality: the Sloan accrual channel flags which names' short-term moves are more likely sentiment noise prone to reverting.
Half-year momentum interacted with profitability: momentum in high-ROE firms is more likely driven by genuinely improving fundamentals and less likely a crowded, fragile trade.
9-month quality-momentum interaction: profitable firms' price trends are less likely pure multiple expansion, so they persist more than momentum in low-ROE names.
Annual quality-momentum interaction: a full year of gains backed by high profitability is a more durable continuation signal than the same gains in a low-ROE firm.
52-week-high-style anchoring (126-day) kept only when operating margin is improving year-over-year, so the underreaction signal reflects genuinely improving economics, not just multiple expansion.
9-month-high anchoring conditioned on margin trend: continuation near a high is more credible when unit economics are simultaneously improving.
Classic 52-week-high anchoring gated by margin improvement: filters the George-Hwang effect to firms whose highs are backed by real operating progress.
Monthly range position weighted by capital efficiency: trading near the top of the range is a more credible continuation signal for firms that also use assets efficiently.
Quarterly range position weighted by asset turnover: operationally efficient firms near their recent highs are less likely mean-reverting on hype alone.
Quarterly momentum kept only when trailing EPS has grown year-over-year: trends backed by genuine earnings growth continue more reliably than sentiment-only rallies.
Half-year momentum confirmed by EPS growth: price trends alongside deteriorating earnings are discounted as more likely to reverse than fundamentally supported ones.
10-day trading range expanding versus its quarterly baseline, signed by trend direction: a volatility breakout in the direction of the move marks a genuine regime shift that continues.
5-day range expansion vs its 2-month baseline, signed by trend: a sudden widening of daily range alongside a directional move signals fresh, broad-based conviction.
Monthly range expansion vs a half-year baseline, signed by trend: a slower-forming volatility breakout in a clear direction reflects a more durable regime change.
Break above/below the monthly average price confirmed by 10-day volume relative to its quarterly baseline: participation surges alongside a break signal durable continuation.
Break of a 2-month average price confirmed by a volume surge relative to a 90-day base: broader participation behind a break is more durable than a break on quiet trading.
Break of a quarterly average price confirmed by rising monthly volume relative to a half-year base: volume-confirmed breaks of longer averages mark more durable regime shifts.
3-day return per unit of dollar volume: a move achieved on thin trading carries a larger price-impact discount and reverts more strongly than the same return on heavy, well-absorbed volume.
Weekly return per unit of dollar volume: an Amihud-style illiquidity measure where thin-volume moves are more likely to be temporary price impact that reverts.
10-day return per unit of dollar volume: captures illiquidity-driven overreaction over a slightly longer window, where thin-volume gains are prone to reversal.
Monthly best-vs-worst-day asymmetry, inverted: stocks with lottery-like positive skew are systematically overpriced by skew-seeking investors and subsequently underperform (the MAX effect).
2-month skew asymmetry, inverted: names whose upside is dominated by one outsized day rather than steady gains are overpriced lottery tickets that underperform.
Quarterly skew asymmetry, inverted: persistent positive-skew payoff profiles command a valuation premium from lottery-seeking investors and subsequently underperform.

Monthly cumulative return after removing each day's cross-sectional average move: momentum in the stock-specific return component reflects firm-level information diffusion, less prone to factor-timing reversals.
Quarterly idiosyncratic momentum: isolating the market-neutral component of the trend captures genuine firm-specific underreaction rather than shared beta exposure.
Half-year idiosyncratic momentum: a durable firm-specific trend, net of market-wide moves, reflects gradual diffusion of company-level information.
3-day idiosyncratic reversal: with market-wide moves removed, the remaining firm-specific overreaction mean-reverts within days independent of broad market swings.
Weekly idiosyncratic reversal: isolating stock-specific order-flow overreaction from market beta gives a cleaner short-horizon reversal signal.
Quarterly momentum scaled by 1-month idiosyncratic volatility: firm-specific trends achieved with low stock-specific risk reflect steadier demand and continue more reliably.
Half-year momentum scaled by 2-month idiosyncratic volatility: low firm-specific noise behind a long trend signals genuine information-driven persistence.
Annual momentum scaled by quarterly idiosyncratic volatility: the year-long trend is more trustworthy when the firm-specific noise behind it has recently been low.
Average daily cross-sectional return-rank over 10 days: consistently ranking near the top day after day indicates durable relative strength that persists.
Average daily cross-sectional rank over a month: smoothed relative strength is a more robust continuation signal than a single large move.
Average daily cross-sectional rank over 2 months: captures durable outperformance versus peers, which tends to persist as institutional flows chase relative strength.
10-day volume-weighted average return: weighting each day by its participation emphasizes high-conviction days over quiet drift, giving a cleaner continuation signal.
Monthly volume-weighted average return: a trend driven by high-volume up-days is more likely genuine accumulation than an equal-weighted average would show.
2-month volume-weighted average return: emphasizes the days where the market voted with real size, a cleaner continuation signal than raw price change.
10-day return-volume covariance: positive co-movement of price changes with volume indicates directional conviction accompanied by participation, distinguishing trends from thin, choppy action.
Monthly return-volume covariance: unlike a correlation, the unnormalized covariance also captures whether the co-movement is happening at meaningful scale.
True compounded monthly return via geometric compounding: captures what a trend-following position would have actually earned including volatility drag, and this realised momentum continues.
Compounded quarterly return: geometric compounding better reflects actual realised momentum than a simple sum, especially for higher-volatility names.
Compounded half-year return: the true realised growth rate over this horizon is a cleaner continuation signal than an additive approximation.
Compounded annual return: the actual realised 1-year growth factor, capturing volatility drag that a simple return sum would miss.
Recency-weighted average sign of daily returns over 10 days: a stock going up on most days, especially recently, reflects a steady grind that continues, distinct from a magnitude measure.
Recency-weighted sign consistency over a month: emphasizes whether the most recent days have been grinding higher, a persistence signal robust to one large outlier day.
Recency-weighted sign consistency over 2 months: a longer-horizon steadiness measure that filters out magnitude-driven noise from a handful of big days.
Recency-weighted close-location-value over 5 days: closing consistently in the upper part of the daily range reflects sustained buying pressure into the close that precedes continued strength.
Recency-weighted close-location-value over 10 days: a stock closing strong within its daily range session after session shows building demand into the close.
Recency-weighted close-location-value over a month: sustained strong closes relative to the day's range is a durable accumulation signal that continues.
Ratio of 10-day to quarterly volatility, signed by recent trend direction: a volatility squeeze resolving in a clear direction often marks the start of a new trending phase.
Ratio of monthly to half-year volatility, signed by trend: a slower-forming squeeze breaking out in a clear direction reflects a durable regime shift.
Monthly cumulative return after clipping daily moves to a modest band: momentum built from many moderate days rather than a few extreme jumps is less likely event-driven and continues more reliably.
Quarterly clipped-return momentum: capping outlier days isolates the steady, information-diffusion-driven part of the trend from single-event noise.
Half-year clipped-return momentum: a robust trend measure less dominated by any single earnings-surprise day, directly targeting the discreteness channel.
3-day return clipped before ranking for reversal: bounding out extreme moves that likely reflect real news isolates the liquidity-driven overreaction component that reliably bounces back.
Weekly clipped-return reversal: moderate, non-extreme short-term swings are the ones most likely driven by transient flow rather than information, and they revert.
5-day trading range vs its 2-month baseline, inverted: recently expanded range reflects elevated idiosyncratic volatility, which the low-volatility literature links to lower subsequent returns.
10-day range vs its quarterly baseline, inverted: names whose range has recently widened carry elevated idiosyncratic risk that is hard to arbitrage and earns lower average returns.
Combines half-year momentum rank with an inverse 1-month volatility rank: stocks trending up with low realised volatility capture both the momentum premium and the low-volatility anomaly jointly.
Combines annual momentum rank with an inverse quarterly volatility rank: trending, low-vol names predict stronger continuation than either factor alone.
Combines half-year momentum rank with an inverse price-to-book rank: cheap stocks catching a bid capture the value and momentum premia jointly, which combine better than either alone.
Annual momentum combined with an inverse price-to-book rank: a cheap stock in a durable uptrend suggests fundamentally supported re-rating rather than a crowded growth trade.
Quarterly momentum down-weighted for high-accrual firms: high accruals predict future negative earnings surprises (Sloan), so momentum in these names is more likely to reverse.
Half-year momentum discounted by accrual quality: earnings running ahead of cash flow signals a fragile trend more prone to reversing than low-accrual momentum.
Monthly range position discounted by leverage: a levered firm near its recent highs is more exposed to sudden distress-driven reversals than a low-leverage firm at the same relative position.
Quarterly range position discounted by leverage: the continuation signal from trading near a recent high is weaker for highly levered names carrying more balance-sheet risk.
Quarterly risk-adjusted momentum interacted with asset turnover: operationally efficient firms have more predictable cash flows, so their risk-adjusted trends more likely reflect real information.
Half-year risk-adjusted momentum weighted by capital efficiency: durable, low-vol trends in operationally strong firms are less likely a fragile, crowded trade.
Half-year momentum jointly ranked with return-on-assets: momentum in a profitable-asset-base firm more likely rides a genuinely improving business than speculative re-rating.
Annual momentum jointly ranked with ROA: a full year of gains backed by strong asset profitability is more durable than the same gains in a low-ROA firm.
3-day reversal kept only when operating margin has improved year-over-year: a sharp swing in an operationally healthy business is more likely a temporary dislocation that reverts.
Weekly reversal filtered by margin stability: the same-size swing amid deteriorating margins may reflect real news that should not be faded as hard.
9-month-high proximity discounted by leverage: anchoring-driven continuation near a high is more durable for low-leverage firms than for highly levered ones facing distress risk.
52-week-high proximity discounted by leverage: the classic anchoring effect is a more trustworthy continuation signal when the firm is not simultaneously carrying elevated financial risk.
Combines quarterly range position with an inverse price-to-book rank: trading near the top of the range while still cheap on book value suggests a fundamentals-supported re-rating.
Percentile position within an ultra-short 3-day range, inverted: at this horizon a close pinned at the extreme more often reflects a transient squeeze than new information, and it reverts.
5-day range position, inverted: an extreme position within such a short window is dominated by liquidity noise rather than genuine trend, so it mean-reverts.
Fast vs slow exponential average of daily returns: an accelerating average return signals strengthening momentum that continues, while deceleration often precedes a stall.
Monthly vs quarterly EMA of daily returns: captures whether the pace of gains is picking up or fading, a leading indicator of trend continuation versus exhaustion.
2-month vs half-year EMA of daily returns: a slower-forming acceleration in average daily return signals a durable strengthening of the trend.
Number of days out of the last month the close was above its quarterly average: persistence above a slower trend line, measured as a simple count, is a robust trend-durability signal.
Days above the half-year average over the last 2 months: a stock spending most recent sessions above its slow trend line shows durable strength that continues.
5-day Kaufman efficiency ratio: net return divided by total path length measures how directly price travelled; an efficient, low-noise move predicts continuation over a choppy one.
10-day efficiency ratio: a high ratio means the stock travelled directly to its net return rather than churning, a hallmark of a genuine, continuing trend.
Monthly efficiency ratio: distinguishes a smooth, low-noise path to a given return (likely to continue) from a churny one achieving the same net move (likely to stall).
2-month efficiency ratio: a durable, direct path over this horizon reflects steady one-directional demand rather than a volatile tug-of-war ending near the same place.
Quarterly efficiency ratio: a high ratio over 3 months signals a low-noise institutional accumulation pattern that is more likely to persist than a choppy retail-driven one.
Half-year efficiency ratio: the longest-horizon directness measure, identifying slow, steady trends least likely to have already reversed course multiple times.
Ratio of a 2-week EMA to its own double-smoothed version: the double-smoothed line lags further, so a single EMA still above it means the trend is still accelerating, not plateauing.
Monthly EMA vs its double-smoothed version: this configuration signals the trend still has forward momentum rather than having already matured and flattened.
2-month EMA vs its double-smoothed version: a persistent gap between the two indicates the medium trend is still building rather than exhausting.

Monthly range position after removing the cross-sectional average range-position that day: isolates whether a stock is unusually strong or weak relative to the typical name, filtering out market-wide range dynamics.
Quarterly range position net of the cross-sectional average: a cleaner relative-strength signal than raw range position, since it strips out days when the whole market is trending together.
Price relative to its 10-day volume-weighted average price: trading persistently above VWAP means the most recent, highest-conviction trades are at ever-higher prices, a hallmark of genuine demand.
Price relative to its monthly VWAP: sustained trading above the volume-weighted average signals durable buying interest rather than a move inflated by a few illiquid prints.
Price relative to its 2-month VWAP: a longer-horizon version of the VWAP-premium continuation signal, capturing more durable participation-weighted demand.

3-day return scaled by 2-week volatility, inverted: at this short horizon the same risk-adjusted statistic that signals durable momentum over long windows instead flags vol-adjusted overreaction that reverts (Nagel-style liquidity provision).
Weekly return scaled by its own recent volatility, inverted: a large move relative to typical risk is compensation for providing liquidity, and it reverts within days.
3-day return scaled by monthly volatility, inverted: normalizing the reversal signal by a slower-moving risk estimate isolates genuinely outsized short-term moves that bounce back.
Proximity to the half-year high confirmed by elevated relative volume: the anchoring effect is strongest when fresh highs are made on above-average participation, not thin conviction.
52-week-high proximity confirmed by volume percentile: broad-based participation behind a new high makes the underreaction-driven continuation signal more reliable.
Quarterly momentum weighted toward lower-dollar-volume names: even within the S&P 500, relatively less-liquid names are slower to fully impound information, so their momentum persists longer.
Half-year momentum weighted toward lower-liquidity large caps: within-universe liquidity differences still predict how quickly momentum decays, even among S&P 500 names.

3-day return, inverted, scaled by the typical monthly daily trading range: normalizing by a stock's characteristic range rather than close-to-close volatility isolates overreaction relative to its usual intraday noise.
Weekly return, inverted, scaled by the typical 2-month daily range: captures reversal magnitude in units of how far this specific stock normally travels each day.
Combines a long-horizon momentum rank with an inverse weekly return rank: a stock in a strong uptrend that has pulled back over the last few days ('buy the dip') tends to resume its primary trend.
Half-year momentum rank combined with an inverse 3-day return rank: isolates a brief liquidity-driven dip within an established uptrend that should resolve back toward the trend.
Quarterly momentum combined with an inverse weekly return rank: a short-term pullback inside a shorter-horizon established trend is a tactical continuation entry, not a reversal.
Dollar gap to the half-year high scaled by a rough dollar-volatility unit: expresses how many typical daily moves a stock is below its high on a like-for-like risk basis across names.
Dollar gap to the 52-week high scaled by dollar volatility: compares anchoring-driven continuation potential across high- and low-volatility names on equal risk terms.
5-day price-volume correlation, inverted: when a short-term price rise is not confirmed by a rising volume trend, the move is more likely a temporary squeeze than durable demand, and it reverses.
10-day price-volume correlation, inverted: a weak or negative link between price and volume over this window flags an unconfirmed move prone to reverting.

Percentile rank of today's return within its own trailing 5-day distribution: an unusually strong day relative to the stock's very recent history reflects fresh, salient news that attracts follow-through buying.
Percentile rank of today's return within its trailing 2-week distribution: a standout day in this context signals a shock still being digested by slower participants, predicting continued drift.
Percentile rank of today's return within its trailing month: a day that stands out against a full month of history reflects a genuinely salient shock, and salient news is underreacted to initially.

Percentile rank of today's idiosyncratic return within a 5-day window, inverted: an idiosyncratically extreme single day for a large-cap stock is more often a temporary overreaction to a discrete event that partially reverses.
Percentile rank of today's idiosyncratic return within 10 days, inverted: firm-specific standout days (earnings, guidance) tend to be overreactions in mature large caps that partially correct.
Half-year momentum kept only for firms deleveraging year-over-year: a falling leverage trend signals improving balance-sheet quality and lowers the risk of a sudden momentum crash.
Annual momentum filtered by a deleveraging trend: firms simultaneously levering up while trending are more exposed to a distress-driven reversal, so their momentum is discounted.

3-day reversal amplified for higher-EPS, more mature firms: well-covered established earners' short-term swings are more likely pure sentiment noise than the genuine information a less-covered name's move might carry.
Weekly reversal amplified for higher-EPS firms: mature, well-understood businesses see short-term price swings that are more likely liquidity noise than a lower-EPS, less-covered name's move.
Plain 2-month cumulative return: the baseline continuation effect from gradual, sequential incorporation of firm-specific information into price over this horizon.
Plain 4-month cumulative return: captures medium-horizon underreaction-driven drift at a window between the classic 1-month and 6-month formulations.
Plain 8-month cumulative return: a slower-decaying continuation signal reflecting information that takes most of a year to be fully priced in.

Change in the monthly rolling high over the last 10 days: a rolling high that is itself still rising shows a sequence of higher highs, a more robust uptrend structure than a single stale high-water mark.
